subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that the determinant with rows (a, b, c), (a², b², c²) and (a³, b³, c³) is equal to abc(a−b)(b−c)(c−a).

mark_split.label: Take a, b, c common from the columns

Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Rearrange to the required form" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this determinant identity — name each operation you would do, in order, and say what comes out at the end.

steps.label: Write the determinant
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own, but write it. Naming the left side Δ means every later line can start with '=' instead of copying the whole determinant again.
steps.memory_tip: Name the left side Δ so every later line can begin with '=' instead of recopying the determinant.

lines.text: \Delta = \text{L.H.S} = \begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ a^3 & b^3 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the working starts from the left-hand side determinant. Naming it is full credit — there is nothing to compute yet.
accept: first I write the left hand side determinant
start by writing delta equals the given determinant
take LHS as the determinant with a b c in the first row
modata LHS determinant rasta
write down the determinant we are asked to prove

steps.why: Every step after this one changes the determinant without changing its value. Writing it once at the top is what makes that chain readable.
common_mistakes: Writing the right-hand side and working backwards; the question says show LHS = RHS.
Copying the full determinant on every line instead of naming it Δ.

steps.label: Take a, b, c common
steps.margin_note: The first mark. Column 1 is a, a², a³ — every entry has an a, so a comes out. Same for b in column 2 and c in column 3. This is the move that turns the powers into the standard pattern.
steps.memory_tip: Column 1 is a, a², a³ — every entry carries an a, so a comes out. Same for b and c.
lines: Taking a, b, c common from C₁, C₂, C₃:

lines.text: \Delta = abc \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That a is taken common from the first column, b from the second and c from the third, leaving abc outside and a row of 1s on top. Saying 'take common' without naming columns is partial.
accept: take a common from the first column b from the second and c from the third so abc comes outside
each column has a common factor a b and c so pull abc out and the top row becomes one one one
take abc common from the three columns leaving one one one in the first row
first column lo a common, second lo b, third lo c so abc bayataki vasthundi
pull a b c out of the columns and you get abc times the determinant with ones on top

steps.why: A common factor comes out of a COLUMN (or a row), never out of the whole determinant at once. Three columns each give one factor, so abc comes out — not a³b³c³.
common_mistakes: Taking a, b, c out of the rows instead of the columns.
Writing a³b³c³ outside — each column gives its factor once only.
Forgetting that the top row becomes 1, 1, 1 after the factor leaves.

steps.label: Do C₂−C₁ and C₃−C₁
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Subtracting column 1 from the other two puts two zeros in the top row. A determinant with two zeros in one row is cheap to expand, and that is the whole point of the move.
steps.memory_tip: Subtracting column 1 puts two zeros in the top row, which makes the expansion cheap.
lines: C₂ → C₂ − C₁ and C₃ → C₃ − C₁:

lines.text: \Delta = abc \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a & b-a & c-a \\ a^2 & b^2-a^2 & c^2-a^2 \end{vmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That column 1 is subtracted from column 2 and from column 3, which makes the first row 1, 0, 0. Both operations must be named.
accept: apply C two minus C one and C three minus C one so the first row becomes one zero zero
subtract the first column from the second and the third to get two zeros in the top row
do column two minus column one and column three minus column one
C2 ki C1 teesi, C3 ki kuda C1 teeste first row one zero zero avthundi
take away column one from both the other columns so the top row is one zero zero

steps.why: Adding or subtracting one column from another leaves a determinant's value unchanged. So you may buy zeros for free, and zeros are what make the expansion short.
common_mistakes: Doing C₁ − C₂ instead of C₂ − C₁ and getting the sign of the answer wrong.
Changing column 1 as well; the column you subtract BY must stay as it is.
Multiplying a column by a number and forgetting to divide the determinant by it.

steps.label: Factorise the bottom row
steps.margin_note: Third mark. b²−a² and c²−a² are differences of squares. Writing them as products is what exposes the (b−a) and (c−a) that come out on the next line.
steps.memory_tip: b²−a² and c²−a² are DIFFERENCES OF SQUARES — writing them as products exposes the brackets.

recall.must_convey: That b²−a² and c²−a² are written as (b−a)(b+a) and (c−a)(c+a), so that each column now has a visible common factor.
accept: write b squared minus a squared as b minus a into b plus a and the same for c
factorise the last row using difference of squares so each column shows b minus a and c minus a
split b square minus a square into b minus a times b plus a
difference of squares formula use chesi b minus a into b plus a ga rasta
break the bottom entries into products so the common factor shows up

steps.why: You cannot take a factor out of a column until it is visibly a factor of every entry in that column. Factorising is what makes it visible.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the bracket out again instead of leaving it as a product.
Writing b² − a² = (b−a)² — that is wrong; it is (b−a)(b+a).
Factorising only one of the two columns.

steps.label: Take (b−a) and (c−a) common
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Column 2 now has (b−a) in both non-zero entries and column 3 has (c−a). Both come out, and the determinant left behind is small enough to expand by eye.
steps.memory_tip: (b−a) comes out of column 2 and (c−a) out of column 3.
lines: Taking (b−a) from C₂ and (c−a) from C₃:

recall.must_convey: That (b−a) comes out of column 2 and (c−a) out of column 3, leaving 1 and 1 in the middle row.
accept: take b minus a common from the second column and c minus a from the third column
pull out b minus a and c minus a so the middle row becomes one and one
b minus a and c minus a come outside leaving a simple determinant
second column nunchi b minus a, third nunchi c minus a common teesukuntam
the two brackets come out in front and the middle entries become ones

steps.why: This is the same move as step 2, used a second time. Recognising that a determinant proof is usually 'make a common factor appear, then take it out, repeat' is what makes the whole chapter one method instead of six tricks.
common_mistakes: Taking (b−a) out of the row instead of the column.
Leaving the (b+a) and (c+a) behind in the wrong row.
Taking the factor out twice — it leaves the column once.

steps.label: Expand along the first row
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. The top row is 1, 0, 0, so only the first term survives. The minor is the bottom-right 2×2 block, and its value is (c+a)·1 − (b+a)·1.
steps.memory_tip: The top row is 1, 0, 0, so only the first term survives; the minor is the bottom-right 2×2.

recall.must_convey: That the determinant is expanded along the first row, and because that row is 1, 0, 0 only one 2×2 minor survives — giving (c+a) − (b+a).
accept: expand along the first row and since it is one zero zero only one minor is left
the two zeros kill the other terms so we get c plus a minus b plus a
expand by the top row to get the two by two determinant c plus a minus b plus a
first row lo zeros unnai kabatti oke term migulutundi
open the determinant along the first row only the one gives a term

steps.why: Expanding along a row with zeros is the reason for every earlier step. Two zeros turn a three-term expansion into a one-term expansion.
common_mistakes: Expanding along a row or column that has no zeros and creating three terms of work.
Getting the minor wrong — it is the block left after deleting the 1's own row and column.
Losing the factors already taken outside.

steps.label: Simplify the bracket
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The a inside the bracket cancels: (c+a) − (b+a) = c − b. One line, but it is a marked line, so write it out rather than doing it in your head.
steps.memory_tip: The a inside cancels: (c+a) − (b+a) = c − b. Write the line out — it is marked.

recall.must_convey: That the a values cancel inside the bracket, leaving c − b.
accept: the a cancels so c plus a minus b plus a is just c minus b
inside the bracket a goes away leaving c minus b
simplify to get c minus b
a cancel aipoyi c minus b migulutundi
both a terms cancel and we are left with c minus b

steps.why: This cancellation is why the answer has three brackets and not four. The a that was added to both terms was never going to survive.
common_mistakes: Writing (c+a) − (b+a) = c − b + 2a by forgetting to distribute the minus sign.
Skipping the line and losing a marked step.

steps.label: Rearrange to the given form
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. The answer is already correct, but the question asked for (a−b)(b−c)(c−a). Flipping (b−a) to −(a−b) and (c−b) to −(b−c) uses two minus signs, and two minus signs cancel — so the value does not change.
steps.memory_tip: The answer is right but not in the asked form. Two sign flips turn (b−a)(c−b) into (a−b)(b−c).
lines: Two sign changes cancel each other.

recall.must_convey: That the brackets are rewritten into the order the question asked for, and that the two sign flips cancel so the value is unchanged. Just saying 'hence proved' is not enough.
accept: flip b minus a to minus a minus b and c minus b to minus b minus c so the two minus signs cancel
rearrange the brackets into a minus b b minus c c minus a using two sign changes that cancel
change the order of the brackets with two minus signs which cancel to give the required form
rendu minus signs cancel avthai so abc into a minus b b minus c c minus a vasthundi
write it as abc a minus b b minus c c minus a which is the right hand side

steps.why: An examiner is looking for the exact form the question named. Reaching an equal but differently-ordered answer and stopping there is the commonest way to drop the last mark on this question.
common_mistakes: Stopping at abc(b−a)(c−a)(c−b) and never writing the asked-for form.
Flipping only one bracket, which changes the sign of the answer.
Writing 'hence proved' with no final line to point at.

insider_note: Take a, b and c out of the COLUMNS first, which is where the abc comes from. Column subtractions then leave (b − a) and (c − a) as the remaining common factors.
